tool.name: Java
tool.tagline: Statically typed, object-oriented language for the JVM, from backends to Android
tool.description: Java is a statically typed, object-oriented language that compiles to bytecode for the Java Virtual Machine, so the same program runs on any platform. It powers a huge share of backend services, big-data systems and Android apps, with a mature ecosystem of libraries, frameworks and tools. Learning it teaches you solid type-driven design and gives you access to one of the most in-demand platforms in industry.

glossary.def: Java Development Kit: the package you install to write Java. It contains the compiler (javac), the JVM that runs programs, and helper tools such as jshell.
Java Virtual Machine: the program that runs compiled Java code (bytecode). There is one for each kind of computer, so the same compiled program runs everywhere.
The Java compiler command. It checks your .java files and turns them into .class files of bytecode.
An interactive prompt that comes with the JDK: type a line of Java, press Enter, and see the result straight away.
One of Java's eight simple built-in kinds of value: int, long, short, byte, double, float, boolean and char. A variable of a primitive type holds the value itself.
Any Java type that isn't a primitive, such as String, arrays and your own classes. A variable of this type holds a reference (an address) to an object, or null.
A class such as Integer or Double that holds one primitive value as an object, so it can be null or go where only objects are allowed.
Java's automatic conversion between a primitive value and its wrapper object, e.g. from int 5 to Integer 5 (boxing) and back (unboxing).
A Java class for building text piece by piece. Unlike a String it can be changed, so adding to it many times doesn't create a new object each time.
Multi-line text written in Java code between triple double quotes ("""). Indentation shared by all lines is removed automatically.
A Java switch that produces a value, written with arrows (case X -> value). It runs exactly one case and must cover every possible input.
A parameter written like int... values, letting a Java method take any number of arguments; inside the method they arrive as an array.
The error Java throws when code uses a variable holding null as if it referred to an object, for example by calling a method on it.
A placeholder such as %d or %.2f in a printf or format template. It says where to insert the next value and how to show it.
A keyword (public, protected, private, or none, called package-private) that controls which other code may use a class, field or method.
Keeping an object's data private and letting other code change it only through the object's own methods, so the object can enforce its rules.
A rule that must always hold for an object, such as 'the balance is never negative'. A well-designed class checks it in one place so nothing can break it.
A Java class for plain data declared in one line, like record Point(int x, int y). Java writes its constructor, accessor methods, equals, hashCode and toString.
A method every Java object has that returns a number summarising its contents. HashMap and HashSet use it to decide where to keep an item; equal objects must return equal numbers.
A Java exception the compiler makes you deal with: calling code must catch it or declare it with throws. Used for failures outside your control, such as a missing file.
A Java exception the compiler doesn't force you to handle: a subclass of RuntimeException, usually signalling a bug or invalid input.
A form of Java's try, written try (var r = ...) { }, that automatically closes files and other resources when the block ends, even after an error.
Java's built-in containers for groups of objects, in java.util: lists, sets, maps and queues, each defined by an interface with several implementations.
Java's standard list: an ordered, growable sequence of objects that you can read by index.
Java's standard map (HashMap) and set (HashSet). They find items very quickly by using each key's hashCode, and keep no particular order.
A Java interface with exactly one abstract method, such as Runnable or Comparator. A lambda can be used anywhere one is expected.
A short way to pass an existing method where a lambda is expected, written with two colons, e.g. String::length or System.out::println.
Describes a local variable that is never reassigned after it is first set. Java lambdas may only use local variables of this kind from the surrounding code.
A Java container that holds either one value or nothing. Methods return it to make 'might be missing' explicit instead of returning null.
A step in a Java stream pipeline, such as filter or map, that describes work but does nothing until a terminal operation runs.
The final step of a Java stream pipeline, such as toList, count or forEach. It triggers the work and produces the result.
A widely used Java build tool configured in a pom.xml file. It downloads libraries, compiles, runs tests and packages a project.
A build tool for Java and Kotlin, configured with a script (build.gradle.kts). It downloads libraries, compiles, runs tests and packages a project.
Java ARchive: one zip file bundling compiled .class files and other resources, used to ship Java libraries and applications.
The list of folders and JAR files where the JVM looks for compiled classes when a program runs.
The standard testing framework for Java. You write test methods marked @Test; JUnit runs them and reports which ones fail.
A tag starting with @, such as @Override or @Test, attached to a class, method or field. It adds information that the compiler or a framework reads.
A program's ability to look at its own classes, methods and fields while it runs, and to use them by name.
A Java class or interface that lists exactly which types may extend it (with permits), so the compiler knows every possible subtype.
A Java pattern such as Point(int x, int y) in a switch or instanceof: it checks that a value is that record and pulls out its parts in one step.
How Java implements generics: the compiler checks the type parameters, then removes them, so while running a List<String> is just a List.
A generic type with a ? in it, such as List<? extends Number>, meaning 'a list of some type that fits this bound'.
A Java object that accepts tasks and runs them on threads it manages, so you don't create and manage threads yourself.
A Java object standing for a result that isn't ready yet; calling get() waits until it is.
A Java Future you can chain further steps onto (thenApply, thenCombine...) that run when the result arrives, instead of waiting for it.
A lightweight thread managed by the JVM (Java 21+). When it waits for input or output it steps aside, so millions can exist at once.
A Java thread backed one-to-one by an operating-system thread. Each is fairly expensive, so a program can have only a few thousand.
One of the few platform threads that virtual threads run on. A virtual thread sits on a carrier while it computes and steps off while it waits.
A Java keyword that lets only one thread at a time run a method or block for a given lock object, and makes its changes visible to the next thread taking that lock.
A thread-safe Java HashMap that many threads can read and update at once, with atomic operations such as merge and computeIfAbsent.
A counter of permits: a thread takes a permit before doing something and gives it back afterwards, which limits how many threads do it at once.
The Java Memory Model's ordering rule: if action A happens-before action B, then B is guaranteed to see everything A did, even on another thread.
The part of the Java specification that says when a change made by one thread is guaranteed to be visible to another.
A Java field modifier: every read sees the latest write from any thread, and writes aren't reordered around it. It does not make x++ atomic.
A starting point the garbage collector treats as always in use, such as the local variables of running methods and static fields. Anything reachable from a root is kept.
Areas of the Java heap. New objects start in the young generation, which is cleaned often; objects that survive long enough move to the old generation.
Java's default garbage collector. It splits the heap into regions and aims to keep each pause shorter than a target time.
A Java garbage collector that does almost all its work while the program keeps running, keeping pauses around a millisecond even for very large heaps.
A JDK tool that prints the contents of a .class file, including its bytecode instructions.
The scratch pile each running JVM method uses: bytecode instructions push values onto it and take them off to compute.
A bytecode instruction whose target is chosen while the program runs, by a setup method; Java uses it for lambdas and string concatenation.
A table inside each .class file holding the names, fixed values and method references its bytecode refers to.
The part of the JVM that finds a class's bytes (in a JAR or folder) and turns them into a usable class the first time it is needed.
Code that runs once, the first time a class is used: its static field assignments and static { } blocks.
The standard JVM in OpenJDK. It interprets bytecode at first and compiles busy code to machine code while the program runs.
HotSpot's strategy of compiling busy code twice: quickly with the C1 compiler for an early speed-up, then with heavy optimisation by C2 for the busiest code.
A compiler optimisation that copies a called method's body into the caller, removing the cost of the call and opening the way to further optimisations.
When the JVM throws away optimised machine code because an assumption behind it turned out false, and falls back to slower code until it recompiles.
A JIT check of whether an object is used only inside one method. If so, the JVM can skip creating it on the heap altogether.
The period after a Java program starts when it runs slower, because the JIT hasn't yet compiled its busy code.
JDK Flight Recorder: a low-overhead recorder built into the JVM that captures events such as CPU samples, memory allocation, GC pauses and lock waits.
Java Microbenchmark Harness: the standard tool for timing small pieces of Java code correctly, handling warm-up and JIT tricks.
A JDK command that sends diagnostic requests to a running JVM, for example to list all threads or save a copy of the heap.
Java Platform Module System (Java 9+): lets a group of packages declare which other modules it needs and which of its packages others may use.
The module that all code on the classpath belongs to. It can read every module, which is why most apps run without a module-info.java.
Short for character set: the rule for turning text into bytes and back, such as UTF-8.
In Java, a group of statements between curly braces { }, such as the body of a method, loop or if. Variables created inside a block exist only there.
A named value that never changes. In Java it is usually a static final variable with an UPPER_CASE name, such as MAX_USERS.
How Java hands arguments to a method: the method gets a copy. For arrays and objects the copy is a reference, so both still point at the same thing.
One of the alternative paths in an if/else or a switch. Only the branch whose condition matches runs.
An object only one thread can hold at a time; other threads that want it wait their turn. Java code takes locks with synchronized blocks or ReentrantLock.
A switch is exhaustive when it has a case for every possible value, so the compiler can prove that nothing is missed.
In a Java module, a package listed with exports in module-info.java. Only exported packages can be used by code in other modules.
A field or method marked static: it belongs to the class itself, not to any one object, and is shared by the whole program.
Short for class loader: the part of the JVM that finds a class's compiled bytes and turns them into a usable class.
To hand a job over to another object or method. A class loader delegates by first asking its parent loader to load a class.
The object a method is called on: in shape.area(), shape is the receiver.
A picture of profiling results: each bar is a method, wider bars used more time, and bars are stacked to show which method called which.
In Java's switch and instanceof, a test of a value's shape, such as String s or Point(int x, int y), that also pulls out its parts when it matches.
Choosing which version of an overridden method to run from the object's actual class, while the program runs, rather than from the variable's declared type.
A method with a body inside a Java interface. Classes implementing the interface get it automatically unless they override it.
Code that introduces a name and says what it is: a variable with its type (int count;), a method with its parameters, or a class.
The rules for which operator is worked out first when an expression has several, e.g. * before +, so 2 + 3 * 4 is 14.
In Java, an object (a Comparator) that decides which of two values comes first; used to sort lists and keep sorted collections in order.

concepts.name: Install the JDK and run code
concepts.summary: Install the JDK, then turn your code into a running program: compile with javac and run with java, or run one file directly.
concepts.why: Every Java program you write goes through these few commands, so knowing what each one does saves hours of confusion.
concepts.body:
A program is a list of instructions for a computer. You write those instructions as ordinary text in a file, and that text is called **source code**. Java source code lives in files whose names end in `.java`.

The computer can't follow Java text directly. A translator first checks your code and converts it into a form that can run. That translator is the **compiler**, and the step is called *compiling*. If the compiler finds a mistake, it stops and prints a **compile error** naming the file and line.

Java's compiler doesn't produce instructions for one particular kind of computer. It produces **bytecode**, a compact set of instructions saved in a `.class` file. A program called the **JVM** (Java Virtual Machine) reads bytecode and carries it out. There is a JVM for Windows, macOS and Linux, so the same `.class` file runs on all of them.

To get the compiler, the JVM and related tools, you install the **JDK** (Java Development Kit). Install a Java 21 build: Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto and the other common builds all ship the same code.

You use these tools by typing commands in a **terminal**: a window where you type a command, press Enter, and read what it prints. Check your install with `java -version`. Then:

- `javac Hello.java` compiles your file and creates `Hello.class`.
- `java Hello` starts the JVM and runs it (no `.class` at the end).
- `java Hello.java` does both in one go, which is handy for small experiments.

To try out single lines, type `jshell`. It lets you type one line of Java at a time: type `2 + 3`, press Enter, and it answers `5`.

Two habits help from day one. Name the file exactly like the class inside it: `Hello` lives in `Hello.java` (the next lesson explains what a class is). And when the compiler reports many errors, fix the first one first; the rest are often knock-on effects of it.

Later you'll probably use an **IDE**, a program for writing code with Java support built in, such as IntelliJ IDEA. It runs these same commands for you.
takeaways: Source code (`.java`) → `javac` compiles it to bytecode (`.class`) → the JVM (`java`) runs it
The JDK bundles the compiler, the JVM and tools such as `jshell`
`java File.java` compiles and runs a single file in one step
pitfalls: Typing `java Hello.class`: the `java` command wants the class name `Hello` (or a `.java` file), not the `.class` file name.

quiz.q: What does `javac Hello.java` produce?
options: A program file that only runs on your own kind of computer
Hello.class containing bytecode for the JVM
A copy of Hello.java with errors fixed
quiz.explain: javac compiles source code into bytecode in a .class file; the java command then runs it on any computer with a JVM.

concepts.name: Anatomy of a Java program
concepts.summary: What every line of Hello World means: the class, the main method, statements, comments and printing text.
concepts.why: You need to read the skeleton of a Java program fluently before anything else makes sense.
concepts.body:
Here is the smallest useful Java program:

```java
public class Hello {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello!");
    }
}
```

All Java code lives inside a **class**. For now, think of a class as a named holder for your code. `public class Hello { ... }` creates a class called `Hello`, and everything between its curly braces `{ }` belongs to it.

Inside the class is a **method**: a named block of instructions. When you run the program, the JVM looks for the method called `main`, written exactly like this, and starts there. Each word has a job:

- `public` means code outside the class may use it (the JVM needs that).
- `static` lets it run without any setup first; the Classes lesson explains this properly.
- `void` means the method gives nothing back when it finishes.
- `String[] args` holds any extra words typed after the program name, its **arguments**. Running `java Hello.java Ana 42` gives `args[0]` = `"Ana"` and `args[1]` = `"42"` (counting starts at 0).

Each instruction inside a method is a **statement**, and each one ends with a semicolon `;`. Statements run one after another, top to bottom. A group of statements between braces is called a **block**.

`System.out.println("Hello!")` prints the text in quotation marks and then starts a new line. `System.out.print` prints without starting a new line. `System.err.println` prints to a separate error output, which the terminal usually shows the same way; use it for error messages.

Java is **case-sensitive**: `System` and `system` are different names, and only the first one works.

Comments are notes for humans that the compiler ignores: `// until the end of the line`, or `/* ... */` across several lines. A `/** ... */` comment above a class or method is used to generate its documentation pages.

Naming conventions aren't enforced, but every Java developer follows them: class names in `PascalCase`, method names in `camelCase`.
takeaways: The program starts at `public static void main(String[] args)`
Statements end with `;`, blocks use `{ }`, and names are case-sensitive
Class names are PascalCase, method names camelCase
pitfalls: Misspelling the main line (e.g. `Main` or `string[]`): the code compiles, but `java` then reports that it can't find a main method.

quiz.q: What does `java Hello.java Bo Cy` put in `args[1]`?
options: Nothing; args has only one entry
quiz.explain: args holds the words typed after the file name, counting from 0: args[0] is "Bo" and args[1] is "Cy".

concepts.name: Variables and primitive types
concepts.summary: Store values in named variables, pick among Java's eight basic types, write number and true/false values, and let var work out the type.
concepts.why: Every value in Java has a type that the compiler checks before the program runs, so choosing types is the first design decision you make.
concepts.body:
A **variable** is a named place that holds a value. You create one by writing its type, a name and usually a starting value. This line is called a **declaration**:

```java
int count = 0;
count = count + 1;   // now 1
```

The type says what kind of value the variable may hold. `int` means a whole number, so `count = "ten";` is rejected by the compiler. Because Java checks types before the program ever runs, it is called **statically typed**. A variable must be given a value before you read it.

Java has eight **primitive types**, the simple kinds of value built into the language:

- `int` for whole numbers up to about ±2.1 billion, and `long` for bigger ones. (`byte` and `short` are smaller and rarely used.)
- `double` for numbers with a fractional part, such as `19.99`. These are **floating-point numbers**, stored approximately. `float` is a less precise version; default to `double`.
- `boolean` for `true` or `false`.
- `char` for a single character, written in single quotation marks: `'A'`.

A value written directly in code is a **literal**. Literals have types too: `42` is an `int`, `42L` a `long`, `3.14` a `double`, `3.14f` a `float`. Underscores make big numbers readable: `1_000_000`.

Text is not a primitive. A piece of text such as `"Ada"` has its own type, `String`, covered two lessons from now.

Instead of writing the type, you can write `var` and let the compiler work it out from the starting value: `var total = 3 * 19.99;` makes `total` a `double`. This is **type inference**. The type is still fixed; `var` just saves typing. Use it when the type is obvious from the right-hand side.

Put `final` in front of a variable that must never change: `final int maxUsers = 100;`. A **constant**, a value for the whole program that never changes, is written in capitals at the top of the class with `static final`, as in the example below.

Watch the limits: an `int` that goes past about 2.1 billion silently wraps around to a large negative number. Use `long` for values that can grow that big, such as a count of milliseconds.
takeaways: 8 primitive types: `byte short int long float double boolean char`; text (`String`) is not one of them
`var` lets the compiler infer a type, but the type is still fixed
`final` stops a variable from changing; `static final` makes a class-wide constant
pitfalls: Forgetting the `L` on a big number: `long big = 5000000000;` is rejected, because without `L` Java reads the number as an `int`, and it's too big for one.

quiz.q: Which statement is true about `var x = 10;`?
options: x is a long because var picks the biggest type
x has no type until it is used
x is an int, fixed before the program runs
quiz.explain: var makes the compiler infer the type int from the value 10, and that type never changes afterwards.

concepts.name: Operators and expressions
concepts.summary: Arithmetic, integer division, comparisons, true/false logic, the ? : shortcut, and converting between number types.
concepts.why: Most mistakes in beginner code come from integer division, the order of operations or comparing the wrong way; this lesson heads them off.
concepts.body:
An **operator** is a sign that does something with values, like `+` or `<`. Values and operators combine into an **expression**, such as `price * 2`, which Java works out to a single value.

The arithmetic operators are `+ - * / %`. One big surprise: when both sides of `/` are whole numbers (`int` or `long`), Java does **integer division** and throws away the fraction. `7 / 2` is `3`, while `7 / 2.0` is `3.5`. `%` gives the remainder (`7 % 2` is `1`), handy for "every second item" logic.

When you mix types, Java converts the smaller one automatically: an `int` plus a `double` gives a `double`. Going the other way needs a **cast**, the target type in brackets, and it can lose information: `(int) 3.99` is `3`. A cast cuts off the fraction; it does not round. Use `Math.round(3.99)` to round.

Shortcuts: `x += 5` means `x = x + 5` (and `-=`, `*=`, `/=` work the same way), and `x++` adds one to `x`. Use `x++` as a statement on its own line rather than inside a bigger expression, where it's easy to misread.

Comparison operators `==  !=  <  <=  >  >=` answer yes or no, so they produce a `boolean`. (`==` means "equal to" and `!=` "not equal to".) `==` compares the numbers themselves. It does *not* reliably compare text; the next lesson shows what to use instead.

The logical operators combine booleans: `&&` (and), `||` (or), `!` (not). `&&` and `||` **short-circuit**: if the left side already decides the answer, the right side is skipped. That's why `count != 0 && total / count > 5` never divides by zero.

The **ternary** operator picks one of two values: `int fee = member ? 0 : 5;` reads as "if member is true then 0, otherwise 5".

Which operator goes first is called **operator precedence**. It follows school maths (`*` before `+`), then comparisons, then `&&`, then `||`. When in doubt, add brackets; readers will thank you.

A mistake that makes a program behave wrongly is called a **bug**, and most beginner bugs hide in exactly these rules.
takeaways: `int / int` loses the fraction; make one side a `double` (e.g. `2.0`) to keep it
A cast like `(int) 3.99` cuts off the fraction; use `Math.round` to round
`&&` and `||` skip the right side when the left side already decides the answer
pitfalls: Computing an average as `sum / count` with two `int`s and silently losing the fraction.

quiz.q: What is the value of `double avg = 5 / 2;`?
quiz.explain: 5 / 2 is worked out as integer division giving 2, which is then converted to 2.0.

quiz.q: In `count != 0 && total / count > 5`, when is the division done?
quiz.explain: && short-circuits: if the left side is false, the right side is skipped.

concepts.name: Strings and text blocks
concepts.summary: Work with text: Strings never change, compare them with equals, use common methods, and build text with StringBuilder and text blocks.
concepts.why: Text is everywhere (what users type, what you print, what you save) and String has a few rules that trip up every newcomer.
concepts.body:
In programming, a piece of text is called a **string**: a string of characters. In Java its type is `String`. Text written in double quotation marks in your code, like `"Ada"`, is a **string literal**.

A String is an **object**: a value that comes with its own built-in methods. You call them with a dot: `name.length()` gives the number of characters, and `name.toUpperCase()` gives an upper-case version. The result a method hands back is its **return value**.

Strings are **immutable**: they never change. `toUpperCase()` doesn't alter `name`; it returns a *new* String. So `name.toUpperCase();` on its own line does nothing useful. Store the result instead: `String loud = name.toUpperCase();`.

Joining strings with `+` is called **concatenation**: `"Hi, " + name + "!"`. Numbers are turned into text automatically: `"Age: " + 31`.

Compare text with `a.equals(b)` (or `equalsIgnoreCase`), never with `==`. A String variable doesn't hold the letters themselves. It holds a **reference**, like an address telling Java where the text is stored. `==` asks "same address?", not "same letters?". It sometimes seems to work, because Java reuses identical literals, and then fails for text that was typed in or built while the program runs.

Useful methods: `charAt(i)` (the character at position `i`, counting from 0), `substring(start, end)` (end not included), `indexOf`, `contains`, `startsWith`, `strip()` (removes spaces at both ends), `isBlank()`, `split(",")` and `repeat(n)`.

`+` is fine for a few pieces. When you add to text many times, for example inside a loop (code that repeats, coming up soon), use a **StringBuilder**: a String you can change. Call `sb.append(x)` as often as you like, then `sb.toString()` at the end.

To fill values into text, use `"%s is %d years".formatted(name, age)`: `%s` takes any value and `%d` a whole number.

Since Java 15, **text blocks** make multi-line text easy. They start with `"""` and a new line, and the indentation shared by all lines is removed:

```java
String note = """
    Dear Ana,
    see you "soon".
    """;
```

Inside a text block you can write `"` marks just as they are.
takeaways: Strings are immutable: always use the returned value
Compare contents with `equals`, never `==`
Use `StringBuilder` when adding to text many times, and text blocks for multi-line text
pitfalls: Writing `s.strip();` on its own line and expecting `s` to change.
Comparing what a user typed with `==`: it fails for text created while the program runs.

quiz.q: After `String s = "hi"; s.toUpperCase();` what is s?
quiz.explain: Strings are immutable; toUpperCase returned a new string, which was thrown away here.

concepts.name: if, else and switch
concepts.summary: Make decisions with if/else, and choose among many options with the modern switch, which can produce a value and never falls through.
concepts.why: Almost every program makes decisions, and the modern switch removes a whole family of easy-to-miss mistakes.
takeaways: Arrow-form `switch` runs exactly one case and can produce a value
A switch expression must cover every value; end it with `default`
Use `yield` to hand back the result of a case that has several statements
pitfalls: Using the old `case X:` form and forgetting `break`, so the code runs on into the next case.

quiz.q: What does this print? `int n = 2; String s = switch (n) { case 1 -> "one"; case 2 -> "two"; default -> "many"; }; System.out.println(s);`
quiz.explain: Arrow cases never fall through, so only the matching case's value is produced.

concepts.name: Loops: for, while and for-each
concepts.summary: Repeat work with for, while and do-while loops, and control them with break and continue.
concepts.why: Loops let a few lines of code handle a thousand items, or keep asking until an answer is valid.
concepts.body:
Often you want the computer to do the same thing many times: add up 100 numbers, print every line, keep asking until the user types something valid. A **loop** repeats a block of code. Each time round the loop is one **iteration**.

The **for** loop is for counting:

```java
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    System.out.println(i);   // 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
}
```

The part in brackets has three pieces separated by semicolons: a starting step (`int i = 1`), a condition checked before every iteration (`i <= 5`), and an update run after each one (`i++`). When the condition becomes false, the loop ends.

The **while** loop is for when you don't know in advance how many times. It repeats as long as its condition stays true: `while (balance < goal) { balance = balance * 1.05; years++; }` keeps going until the goal is reached. Make sure something inside changes the condition, or the loop never ends.

The **do-while** loop is the same, except that the condition is checked at the end, so the body always runs at least once. That suits "ask, then check the answer".

Two special words control a loop from the inside:

- `break` leaves the loop immediately.
- `continue` skips the rest of this iteration and goes on to the next one.

A variable created in the `for` brackets (`int i`) exists only inside that loop. If you need its final value afterwards, create the variable before the loop.

Off-by-one mistakes are the classic loop bug. When counting from 0, a loop over `n` items is `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)`, with `<`, not `<=`. Java numbers the positions in a group of values from 0, as the next lesson shows.

There is one more loop, the **for-each** loop, which visits every value in a group without any counting. It's introduced with arrays in the next lesson.
takeaways: `for` when you count, `while` when you repeat until something changes
`do-while` always runs its body at least once
`break` leaves the loop; `continue` jumps to the next iteration
pitfalls: Off-by-one: `for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++)` runs n + 1 times, not n.

quiz.q: How many times does `do { x++; } while (x < 0);` run its body when x starts at 5?
quiz.explain: do-while checks its condition after the body, so the body always runs at least once.

concepts.name: Arrays
concepts.summary: Keep many values in one fixed-size array, reach each by its position, visit them with for-each, and print, sort and copy with Arrays.
concepts.why: Whenever a program handles many values of the same kind (scores, names, readings) it needs a way to keep them together.
concepts.body:
An **array** holds a fixed number of values of one type, in order, like a set of numbered lockers. Create one with a size, or with its starting values:

```java
int[] scores = new int[5];            // five ints, all 0 to start
String[] names = {"Ana", "Bo", "Cy"};
```

Each slot has a position number, its **index**. Indexes start at 0: `names[0]` is `"Ana"` and `names[2]` is `"Cy"`. Counting from 0 like this is called **zero-based indexing**. The length is `names.length` (no brackets after `length`), and the last index is always one less than the length. Reading `names[3]` stops the program with an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` error, because Java always checks.

A new array is filled with **default values**: `0` for numbers, `false` for booleans, and `null` for Strings. **null** means "refers to nothing yet".

To visit every value, use the **for-each** loop. It needs no index, so it can't go one step too far:

```java
for (String name : names) {
    System.out.println("Hi " + name);
}
```

Use a counting `for` loop when you need the position: `for (int i = 0; i < scores.length; i++)`.

Like a String variable, an array variable holds a reference, the address of the array. So `int[] b = a;` copies nothing: `a` and `b` are two names for the *same* array, and changing `b[0]` changes `a[0]`. To make a real copy, use `Arrays.copyOf(a, a.length)`.

An array of arrays makes a grid: `int[][] grid = new int[3][4];` and then `grid[row][col]`.

`Arrays` is a toolbox that comes with Java. To **import** it, that is, make it available in your file, put `import java.util.Arrays;` at the top. Then:

- `Arrays.toString(arr)` gives readable text like `[1, 3, 5]`. Printing an array directly shows something unhelpful like `[I@1b6d3586`.
- `Arrays.sort(arr)` sorts the array itself, smallest first.
- `Arrays.equals(a, b)` compares contents, unlike `==`.

An array can't grow. For groups of values that change size, Java has lists, covered in a later chapter.
takeaways: Indexes run from 0 to `length - 1`
Array variables hold references: `b = a` shares the array, `Arrays.copyOf` copies it
Use for-each to visit every value, and `Arrays.toString`, `sort`, `equals` for common jobs
pitfalls: Printing an array with `println(arr)` and getting `[I@6d06d69c` instead of its contents.

quiz.q: After `int[] a = {1, 2}; int[] b = a; b[0] = 9;` what is `a[0]`?
quiz.explain: a and b refer to the same array, so a change made through b is visible through a.

concepts.name: Methods
concepts.summary: Write your own methods: give them parameters, return a result, reuse a name for different inputs, and see how Java passes values in.
concepts.why: Methods let you name an idea once and reuse it, instead of copying the same lines around.
concepts.body:
You've been calling methods such as `Math.max` and `name.length()`. Now you'll write your own. A method is a named block of code that you can run, or *call*, from elsewhere by its name:

```java
static double area(double width, double height) {
    return width * height;
}
```

Read the first line from left to right. `static`: for now every method you write has it, so that `main` can call it directly. Then the type of result it gives back (`double`, or `void` for nothing), the name, and in brackets its **parameters**: named inputs, each with a type.

When you call `area(3, 4)`, the values `3` and `4` are the **arguments**; they fill in the parameters `width` and `height`. The `return` statement ends the method and hands back its return value, here `12.0`. A method that promises a result must `return` one on every path, and the compiler checks this.

**Overloading** means several methods share a name but take different parameters, such as `describe(int n)` and `describe(String s)`. The compiler picks the one that matches the arguments. Two methods can't differ only in their result type.

**Varargs** let a method take any number of arguments: `static int sum(int... values)`. Inside the method, `values` is an array.

Java always passes *copies* of values into a method; this is called **pass by value**. A number parameter is a copy, so changing it inside the method has no effect outside. An array parameter is a copy of the *reference*. Both copies point at the same array, so the method can change its contents and the caller sees that. But pointing the parameter at a new array changes nothing outside.

Variables created inside a method are **local variables**: they exist only while that call runs, and each call gets a fresh set.

Good methods are short, do one thing, and are named for what they do: `calculateTotal`, `isValid`. Methods that return a boolean usually start with `is`, `has` or `can`.
takeaways: A method has a result type (or `void`), a name and parameters; `return` hands back the result
Overloads share a name but differ in their parameters
Java passes copies of values; for arrays and objects the copy is a reference
pitfalls: Expecting a method that points its parameter at a new array (`arr = new int[3]`) to change the caller's variable.

quiz.q: A method runs `arr[0] = 5; arr = new int[]{7};` on its array parameter `arr`. The caller's array was `{1}`. What is it afterwards?
quiz.explain: The first line changes the shared array through the reference; the second only points the method's own copy of the reference somewhere else.

concepts.name: Wrapper types and boxing
concepts.summary: Wrapper classes such as Double turn basic values into objects: learn the automatic conversion, turning text into numbers, and the null and == surprises.
concepts.why: You turn typed text into numbers in almost every program, and you meet wrapper types as soon as you keep numbers in Java's lists and maps.
concepts.body:
Each primitive type has a matching **wrapper class**: `Integer` for `int`, `Double` for `double`, and likewise `Long`, `Boolean`, `Character` and the rest. A wrapper is an object holding one value. That gives it two powers a plain `int` lacks: it can be `null` (no value at all), and it can go where Java accepts only objects, such as the lists and maps you'll use later.

Java converts between the two forms for you. Putting an `int` where an `Integer` is needed is **autoboxing** (wrapping it in an object); taking the value back out is unboxing:

```java
Integer boxed = 42;     // autoboxing
int plain = boxed + 1;  // unboxing, then adding
```

This convenience hides two surprises.

First, unboxing `null` crashes the program with a `NullPointerException`. An **exception** is how Java reports an error while a program runs: unless some code handles it, the program stops and prints the exception's name and the line where it happened.

Second, `==` on wrappers compares references, just as it does for Strings. Java reuses the objects for small values (−128 to 127), so with `Integer a = 100, b = 100;` the test `a == b` is true, but with 1000 it is usually false. Use `a.equals(b)`, or unbox first.

The wrapper classes also hold handy helpers. The one you'll use daily is **parsing**: reading text and turning it into a value. `Integer.parseInt("42")` gives the `int` 42, and `Double.parseDouble("3.5")` gives 3.5. If the text isn't a number, they throw a `NumberFormatException`.

You can deal with that using `try` and `catch`: the code in `try` runs, and if that exception happens, the `catch` block runs instead of the program stopping. The Exceptions lesson covers this fully.

Going the other way, `String.valueOf(n)` turns a number into text. Other helpers include `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, `Character.isDigit(c)` and `Character.isLetter(c)`.

Prefer plain primitives when you don't need these powers. Every wrapper is a separate object, so a million `Integer`s take several times the **memory** (the computer's working space for running programs) of an `int[]` of the same length.
takeaways: Wrappers like `Integer` hold one value as an object and can be `null`
Compare wrapper values with `equals`, not `==`
`Integer.parseInt` and friends turn text into numbers and throw on bad input
pitfalls: Unboxing an `Integer` that is `null` into an `int` throws NullPointerException.

quiz.q: What happens on `Integer count = null; int n = count;`?
quiz.explain: Unboxing needs a value inside the wrapper; null has none, so Java throws NullPointerException.

concepts.name: Console input and formatted output
concepts.summary: Read what the user types with Scanner or BufferedReader, and print neat, lined-up output with printf.
concepts.why: Small programs you run in a terminal need to read what people type and show results clearly.
concepts.body:
Printing with `System.out.println` is fine for simple output. For neatly lined-up output or a fixed number of decimals, use `System.out.printf`. Its first argument is the text to print, and each `%` code in it is replaced by the next value:

```java
System.out.printf("%-10s %6.2f%n", name, price);
```

These codes are called **format specifiers**. The common ones:

- `%s` any value as text, `%d` a whole number, `%f` a number with decimals.
- `%.2f` exactly two decimals. A number before the letter sets a width: `%8d` right-aligns in 8 characters, `%-10s` left-aligns in 10.
- `%n` a new line, and `%%` a percent sign itself.

The same codes work in `String.format(...)` and `"...".formatted(...)` when you want the text instead of printing it.

Typed input arrives through **standard input**, which Java calls `System.in`. By default that is whatever the user types in the terminal. The simplest way to read it is a `Scanner` (add `import java.util.Scanner;` at the top of the file). Create one once, then ask for each line:

```java
Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);
String line = in.nextLine();   // waits until the user presses Enter
```

Scanner also has `nextInt()`, but it has a classic catch. It reads the number and leaves the Enter key-press behind, so a following `nextLine()` returns an empty line. The reliable habit is to read every answer with `nextLine()` and convert it yourself with `Integer.parseInt(...)`.

Standard input doesn't have to be the keyboard. Running `java App.java < data.txt` feeds the file in as if it were typed. For large inputs like that, Scanner is slow, and `BufferedReader` reads line by line much faster:

```java
var in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in));
String line;
while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) { ... }
```

The `while` condition reads the next line into `line` and checks that it isn't `null`. `readLine()` returns `null` when the input ends: at the end of a file, or when the user presses Ctrl+D (Ctrl+Z then Enter on Windows). Code like this needs `throws IOException` after `main(...)`, a rule the Exceptions lesson explains.

Remember the other way in, too: the arguments typed after the program name (`args`). They suit settings such as a file name, while standard input suits the data itself.
takeaways: `printf` and `formatted` with `%s %d %.2f %n` give precise output
Read whole lines with `nextLine()` and convert them, to avoid Scanner's leftover-Enter problem
Use `BufferedReader` for big inputs; `readLine()` returns null at the end
pitfalls: Calling `nextInt()` then `nextLine()` and getting an empty line.

quiz.q: What does `String.format("%5.1f|", 3.14159)` produce?
quiz.explain: Width 5 with one decimal right-aligns "3.1" in five columns, padding with two spaces.

concepts.name: Classes and objects
concepts.summary: Design your own types: a class lists the data and actions its objects have; create objects with new, and use this, static and null.
concepts.why: Java is built around objects: every real program describes its world (customers, orders, game pieces) as classes.
concepts.body:
So far a class has just been the frame around `main`. Its real job is to be a **blueprint** for your own kind of object. A class `Product` can describe what every product has (a name, a price) and what it can do (be sold). Each actual product you create from it is an object, also called an **instance** of the class.

The data an object holds lives in **fields**: variables written in the class, outside any method. The actions are methods:

```java
class Counter {
    int count;                 // field: each Counter has its own
    void increment() { count++; }
}
Counter c = new Counter();     // create an object
c.increment();                 // now c.count is 1
```

`new Counter()` creates an object and gives back a reference to it. Every object is made with `new`; String literals are a built-in shortcut.

Methods without `static` are **instance methods**: they run on one particular object and can read and change its fields. Inside them, `this` means "the object this method was called on". You only need to write it to avoid confusion, as in `this.name = name`.

**Static members** (fields and methods marked `static`) belong to the class itself and are shared by all its objects. That's why `main` and your earlier methods could run without creating anything. Use `static` for helpers like `Math.max` and for constants, not for data that differs from object to object.

As with arrays, a variable of a class type holds a reference. Two variables can refer to one object, and a change made through one is visible through the other. A variable holding `null` refers to no object, and calling a method on it throws a `NullPointerException`: an error (Java calls it an **exception**) that stops the program and names the line where it happened.

Fields start with default values (`0`, `false`, `null`). Local variables don't: you must set them before use.

Give your classes a `toString()` method that returns readable text. Every class already has one, which prints something like `Counter@1b6d3586`; writing your own version replaces it, and replacing a method that a class gets automatically like this is called **overriding**. Java calls `toString()` automatically in `println` and when joining with `+`.

You never delete objects yourself. When nothing refers to an object any more, the **garbage collector**, part of the JVM, frees its memory automatically.
takeaways: A class defines fields (data) and methods (actions); `new` creates an object
Variables hold references, so several can point at one object
Override `toString()` for readable output
pitfalls: Calling a method through a variable that holds `null` instead of an object, causing NullPointerException.

quiz.q: Two variables `a` and `b` refer to the same Counter object, and you call `b.increment()`. What does `a.count` show?
quiz.explain: There is only one object; both variables are references to it, so the change is visible through either.

concepts.name: Constructors and object setup
concepts.summary: Set up new objects with constructors: overload them, chain them with this(...), and check arguments up front.
concepts.why: Constructors guarantee an object starts life in a valid state, which removes whole categories of bugs.
takeaways: A constructor has the class name, no return type, and runs on `new`
Writing any constructor removes the implicit no-arg one
Chain with `this(...)` and validate arguments so invalid objects never exist
pitfalls: Calling an overridable method from a constructor — the subclass version runs before the subclass is initialised.

quiz.q: A class declares only `Point(int x, int y)`. What happens with `new Point()`?
quiz.explain: Once any constructor is declared the compiler no longer generates the default no-argument one.

concepts.name: Encapsulation and access modifiers
concepts.summary: Hide state behind private fields, expose behaviour through methods, and choose between public, protected, package-private and private.
concepts.why: Encapsulation lets you change a class's internals without breaking the code that uses it.
concepts.body:
**Encapsulation** means a class owns its data: fields are private, and the outside world interacts only through methods that keep the object valid. That way a rule that must always hold, an **invariant** such as "balance is never negative", is enforced in one place instead of hoped for everywhere.

Java has four access levels, set with **access modifiers**:

- `private` — visible only inside the class (including its nested classes).
- *package-private* (nothing written) — visible to classes in the same package, a named group of related classes, like a folder (see the Packages lesson).
- `protected` — package plus subclasses in other packages.
- `public` — visible everywhere.

The rule of thumb: start with the most restrictive level that works, and widen only when needed. Fields are almost always `private`. Helper methods are `private`. Only the operations you are willing to support long-term become `public`.

Getters and setters are common, but don't generate a setter for every field by reflex. A method that expresses intent (`account.deposit(amount)`) is better than `setBalance(getBalance() + amount)` because it can validate and it documents the allowed operations. Fields that should never change after construction should be `private final` with no setter at all.

Be careful when exposing internals that can be changed (**mutable** ones). Returning your internal `List` lets callers modify it behind your back. Return an unmodifiable view or a copy instead, e.g. `List.copyOf(items)`, and copy changeable arguments you store.

An object whose state can't change after construction is **immutable**. Immutable objects are simpler to reason about, can be shared freely, and are naturally **thread-safe** (several threads can use them at once without risk) — `String`, `LocalDate` and records are all designed this way.
takeaways: Make fields `private`; expose meaningful operations, not raw state
Default to the narrowest access level and widen only when needed
Don't leak mutable internals — return copies or unmodifiable views
pitfalls: Adding a public getter and setter for every field, which is barely better than a public field.

quiz.q: A field has no access modifier. Who can access it?
options: Any class in the same package
quiz.explain: No modifier means package-private: visible to code in the same package and nowhere else.

concepts.name: Inheritance and polymorphism
concepts.summary: Extend classes, override methods, call super, and let polymorphism pick the right method while the program runs.
concepts.why: Polymorphism lets one piece of code work with many types, and frameworks and libraries (ready-made code you reuse) are full of inheritance.
concepts.body:
A class can **extend** one other class and get all its fields and methods: `class Dog extends Animal`. This is **inheritance**. `Dog` is the subclass and `Animal` its parent, or **base class** (also called superclass). The subclass can add members and **override** inherited methods to change behaviour. Every class ultimately extends `java.lang.Object`, which is where `toString`, `equals` and `hashCode` come from.

Mark overrides with `@Override`. The compiler then checks that you really override something; without it, a typo like `tostring()` silently creates a new method.

**Polymorphism** is the payoff: a variable of type `Animal` can refer to a `Dog` or a `Cat`, and calling `animal.sound()` runs the override of the object's *actual* class, decided while the program runs, at **runtime** (this is called **dynamic dispatch**). Code written against `Animal` works for subclasses that didn't exist when it was written.

Use `super.method()` to call the parent's version from an override, and `super(...)` as the first statement of a constructor to run the parent's constructor. If you don't, the compiler inserts `super()` — which fails if the parent has no no-arg constructor.

Modifiers that limit inheritance:

- `final` class — can't be extended (`String` is final). `final` method — can't be overridden.
- `abstract` class — you can't create (**instantiate**) objects of it directly, and it may declare `abstract` methods without a body that subclasses must implement.

Inheritance creates tight coupling: subclasses depend on the parent's implementation details. The classic advice is to **prefer composition over inheritance** — hold a reference to a helper object instead of extending it — and keep inheritance for genuine "is-a" relationships. For shared contracts, interfaces (next lesson) are usually the better tool.
takeaways: `extends` inherits members; overriding replaces behaviour for the subclass
Calls dispatch on the object's runtime class, not the variable's type
Always write `@Override`; prefer composition when "is-a" doesn't truly hold
pitfalls: Omitting `@Override` and misspelling the method name, so the parent's version still runs.

quiz.q: `Animal a = new Dog(); a.sound();` — Dog overrides sound(). Which version runs?
options: Animal's, because the variable is an Animal
It doesn't compile without a cast
quiz.explain: Instance method calls are dispatched on the object's actual class at runtime.

quiz.q: What is true of an abstract class?
options: All its methods must be abstract
quiz.explain: An abstract class can have fields, constructors and concrete methods, but you can't call new on it.

concepts.name: Interfaces
concepts.summary: Define contracts with interfaces, implement several at once, and use default and static methods.
concepts.why: Programming to interfaces is the backbone of flexible Java design — collections, JDBC, Spring and testing all rely on it.
concepts.body:
An **interface** declares what a type can do without saying how. A class `implements` it by providing all of its abstract methods:

```java
interface Notifier {
    void send(String to, String message);
}
class EmailNotifier implements Notifier { ... }
```

A class can extend only one class but implement **any number** of interfaces, so interfaces are how Java models capabilities: `Comparable`, `Runnable`, `AutoCloseable`, `Iterable`.

The key habit is **programming to the interface**: declare variables, parameters and return types with the interface type (`List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();`, `Notifier notifier`). Your code then works with any implementation, and swapping one — or injecting a fake in a test — needs no changes.

Since Java 8 interfaces can also contain:

- **default methods** — with a body, inherited by implementations, used to evolve interfaces without breaking existing classes (e.g. `List.sort`).
- `static` methods — utilities related to the interface (e.g. `List.of`, `Comparator.comparing`).
- `private` methods (Java 9+) — helpers shared by default methods.

Interfaces cannot hold instance state; fields declared in them are implicitly `public static final` constants.

An interface with exactly one abstract method is a **functional interface**. It can be implemented with a lambda, a short nameless function, which is a big topic of its own coming up soon.

Interface vs abstract class: use an interface to define a role many unrelated classes can play; use an abstract class when subclasses genuinely share state and implementation. In modern Java, interfaces are the default choice.
takeaways: An interface is a contract; a class can implement many
Declare variables and parameters with interface types
`default` methods add behaviour without breaking implementers
pitfalls: Declaring parameters as concrete classes (`ArrayList`) instead of interfaces (`List`), which makes code rigid.

quiz.q: Why were default methods added to interfaces?
options: To add methods to existing interfaces without breaking their implementations
To let interfaces store per-object state
quiz.explain: Default methods supply a body, so existing implementers keep compiling when an interface gains a method.

concepts.name: Enums
concepts.summary: Model fixed sets of constants with enums that can carry fields, constructors and methods, and switch over them.
concepts.why: Enums replace made-up text or number codes with a fixed list of values the compiler can check.
takeaways: Enums are type-safe, fixed sets of instances that can have fields and methods
Switch expressions over enums can be exhaustive without `default`
Comparing enum constants with `==` is correct
pitfalls: Storing `ordinal()` in a database; reordering constants then corrupts the data.

quiz.q: A switch expression covers every constant of an enum and has no default. What happens when a new constant is added?
options: The new value silently returns null
Nothing; the first case is used
The switch no longer compiles until the new case is handled
quiz.explain: Exhaustiveness is checked at compile time, so the missing case is reported as an error.

concepts.name: Records
concepts.summary: Declare immutable data holders in one line; records generate the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString.
concepts.why: Most applications pass lots of plain data around, and records remove the repetitive code you'd otherwise write by hand while making the data immutable by default.
takeaways: `record R(A a, B b)` generates constructor, accessors, equals/hashCode/toString
Validate or normalise in a compact constructor
Records are shallowly immutable — copy mutable components
pitfalls: Calling `getX()` on a record; accessors are named exactly like the components, e.g. `x()`.

quiz.q: Given `record P(int x) {}`, what does `new P(1).equals(new P(1))` return?
options: It doesn't compile without overriding equals
quiz.explain: Records generate equals based on component values, so equal components mean equal records.

concepts.name: Exceptions
concepts.summary: Throw and catch exceptions, understand checked vs unchecked, and clean up resources with try-with-resources.
concepts.why: Robust programs must handle failure deliberately, and Java's checked exceptions force you to think about it.
concepts.body:
When something goes wrong, Java code **throws** an exception object. Java then leaves the current method, then the method that called it, and so on back along the chain of calls (the **call stack**), until a matching `catch` handles it. If nothing does, the thread ends and Java prints a **stack trace**: the list of method calls that led to the error. Read it from the top: the first line says what happened, the first line mentioning *your* code says where.

The hierarchy matters:

- `Exception` subclasses (except `RuntimeException`) are **checked**: the compiler forces callers to catch them or declare `throws`. Examples: `IOException` (file or network trouble), `SQLException` (database trouble) — failures outside your control.
- `RuntimeException` subclasses are **unchecked**: programming errors or invalid input, such as `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`, `IllegalStateException`.
- `Error` (e.g. `OutOfMemoryError`) signals JVM-level problems you normally don't catch.

Catch the most specific type you can actually handle; combine types with a multi-catch `catch (IOException | ParseException e)`. Never swallow an exception with an empty catch block — at minimum log it.

When you translate a low-level exception into your own, pass the original as the **cause** (`throw new ConfigException("bad config", e)`) so the stack trace keeps the root cause.

`finally` runs whether or not an exception occurred. For things that must be closed after use, such as open files and network or database connections, prefer **try-with-resources**, which closes anything `AutoCloseable` automatically, in reverse order, even on failure:

```java
try (var reader = Files.newBufferedReader(path)) {
    return reader.readLine();
}
```

Use exceptions for exceptional situations, not ordinary control flow; for "not found" results, an `Optional` return is often clearer.
takeaways: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared; unchecked ones signal bugs or bad input
Catch specific types, never swallow silently, and chain the cause when wrapping
try-with-resources closes files and connections automatically
pitfalls: `catch (Exception e) {}` — hides real failures and makes finding their cause miserable.
Wrapping an exception without passing the cause, losing the original stack trace.

quiz.q: Which exception is checked?
quiz.explain: IOException extends Exception but not RuntimeException, so the compiler enforces handling it.

concepts.name: Generics basics
concepts.summary: Use type parameters like List<String> and Map<K, V>, write simple generic classes and methods, and let the diamond infer types.
concepts.why: Generics let the compiler check what goes into every list and map, catching type mistakes before the program runs.
takeaways: Type arguments give compile-time checks and remove casts
Use the diamond `<>` and let the compiler infer
Bounds like `<T extends Comparable<T>>` let generic code call methods on T
pitfalls: Using raw types (`List list = new ArrayList();`) and losing the compiler's checks.

quiz.q: Why does `List<int>` fail to compile?
options: Type arguments must be reference types; use List<Integer>
quiz.explain: Generics work with reference types only; Integer wraps int and autoboxing converts between them.

concepts.name: Lists and the Collections Framework
concepts.summary: Use List, ArrayList and List.of, iterate and sort them, and know when to pick which list implementation.
concepts.why: Lists are the most used way to hold a group of values in Java code; using them idiomatically is a daily skill.
concepts.body:
The **Collections Framework** in `java.util` is Java's set of ready-made holders for groups of objects. Each kind is described by an interface, a list of methods a class promises to provide (`List`, `Set`, `Map`, `Queue`, `Deque`), and implemented by several classes. You write your code against the interface and pick the implementation once, when you create the object.

A **List** is an ordered sequence that allows duplicates and index access. **ArrayList** is the default choice: backed by a resizable array, fast `get(i)` and fast appends. `LinkedList` is rarely the right answer — despite theory, it is slower than `ArrayList` for almost every real workload. For a **queue** (first in, first out) or a stack (last in, first out), use `ArrayDeque`.

Core operations: `add(x)`, `add(i, x)`, `get(i)`, `set(i, x)`, `remove(i)` or `remove(obj)`, `size()`, `isEmpty()`, `contains(x)`, `indexOf(x)`.

Create small fixed lists with `List.of("a", "b")`. These are **unmodifiable**: `add` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, and they reject `null` elements. When you need a copy you can change, write `new ArrayList<>(List.of(...))`.

Sorting: `list.sort(Comparator.naturalOrder())` or with a comparator built from key extractors:

The `->` and `::` below are shorthand explained in later lessons; read `Person::lastName` as "each person's last name".

```java
people.sort(Comparator.comparing(Person::lastName).thenComparing(Person::age));
```

To remove elements matching a condition, use `list.removeIf(x -> x.isBlank())` rather than removing inside a for-each loop, which throws `ConcurrentModificationException`.

Watch `remove` on a `List<Integer>`: `list.remove(1)` removes the element at **index** 1, while `list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1))` removes the value 1.

Since Java 21, `List` is a `SequencedCollection`, giving `getFirst()`, `getLast()`, `removeLast()` and `reversed()`.
takeaways: Declare `List<T>`, construct `ArrayList` — it's the right default
`List.of` is unmodifiable and null-hostile; copy into an `ArrayList` to change it
Sort with `Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...)`; filter out with `removeIf`
pitfalls: Calling `remove(int)` on a `List<Integer>` when you meant to remove a value.

quiz.q: What happens on `List.of(1, 2).add(3)`?
options: It returns false and does nothing
quiz.explain: List.of returns an unmodifiable list; mutating methods throw UnsupportedOperationException.

concepts.name: Maps, Sets and equals/hashCode
concepts.summary: Store key-value pairs in HashMap, unique items in HashSet, and implement equals and hashCode correctly for your keys.
concepts.why: Lookups by key and de-duplication are everywhere, and broken equals/hashCode is one of the most common subtle bugs.
concepts.body:
A **Map** stores **key-value pairs**: you look up a value by its key, like a word in a dictionary. Each key appears at most once. **HashMap** is the default. It is a **hash table**: it turns each key into a number that says where to look, so `put` and `get` stay fast however big the map grows. It keeps no particular order. `LinkedHashMap` keeps insertion order, and `TreeMap` keeps keys sorted.

Idiomatic map code uses the newer methods instead of check-then-act sequences:

- `getOrDefault(key, fallback)` — avoid nulls for missing keys.
- `merge(word, 1, Integer::sum)` — counting in one line.
- `computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(value)` — grouping into lists.
- Iterate with `for (var e : map.entrySet())` and use `e.getKey()`, `e.getValue()`.

A **Set** holds unique elements. `HashSet` is the default, `LinkedHashSet` preserves insertion order, `TreeSet` keeps elements sorted. `set.add(x)` returns `false` if `x` was already present.

Both hash-based structures depend on two methods every object gets from Java's root class `Object`. The contract: if `a.equals(b)` then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()`. The **hash** code (a number computed from the object's contents) picks a slot, called a bucket, and `equals` confirms the match. If you override `equals` but not `hashCode`, two "equal" keys land in different buckets and lookups mysteriously fail.

The easiest way to get both right is to use a **record** or `String` as a key. For a regular class, generate them with your IDE or use `Objects.equals` and `Objects.hash`.

Never change an object in a way that alters its hash code while it is a key in a map or member of a set — it becomes unreachable. Immutable keys avoid this entirely.

`Map.of(...)` and `Set.of(...)` create small unmodifiable collections, and `Set.of` rejects duplicate elements.
takeaways: HashMap/HashSet are the defaults; Linked* keep insertion order, Tree* keep sorted order
Use `merge`, `computeIfAbsent` and `getOrDefault` instead of check-then-put
Equal objects must have equal hash codes — records do this for you
pitfalls: Overriding `equals` without `hashCode`, so equal keys aren't found in a HashMap.
Mutating a key after inserting it into a HashMap or HashSet.

quiz.q: A class overrides equals but not hashCode. What typically happens with `set.contains(equalCopy)` on a HashSet?
options: Usually false, because the copy hashes to a different bucket
quiz.explain: Without a matching hashCode the lookup checks the wrong bucket and never calls equals on the stored element.

concepts.name: Lambdas and functional interfaces
concepts.summary: Pass behaviour as values with lambdas and method references, and use the standard functional interfaces in `java.util.function`.
concepts.why: Much of Java's built-in code, from sorting lists to processing data, expects you to pass in a lambda.
concepts.body:
A **lambda** is a short, nameless function you can pass around as a value. It implements a functional interface (an interface with exactly one abstract method) without writing a whole class: you write just the parameters, an arrow `->` and the body:

```java
Comparator<String> byLength = (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length());
Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("tick");
```

Parameter types are inferred from the target interface. A single parameter needs no parentheses (`s -> s.isBlank()`), and a multi-line body uses braces with an explicit `return`.

`java.util.function` provides the standard shapes, so you rarely need to declare your own:

- `Function<T, R>` — takes T, returns R (`apply`).
- `Predicate<T>` — takes T, returns boolean (`test`).
- `Consumer<T>` — takes T, returns nothing (`accept`).
- `Supplier<T>` — takes nothing, returns T (`get`).
- `BiFunction<T, U, R>`, `UnaryOperator<T>`, `BinaryOperator<T>`, plus versions like `IntPredicate` that work on plain `int`s and avoid autoboxing (wrapping each number in an object).

A **method reference** is shorthand when a lambda just calls an existing method: `String::length`, `System.out::println`, `Person::new`, `this::validate`.

A lambda can use local variables of the surrounding method only if they are **effectively final**: never reassigned after being set. This avoids confusing code where several pieces change the same variable; to add things up, use a stream (next lesson) or a field instead.

Functional interfaces compose: `Predicate.and/or/negate`, `Function.andThen/compose`, `Comparator.thenComparing/reversed`. Annotate your own with `@FunctionalInterface` so the compiler enforces the single-abstract-method rule.
takeaways: A lambda implements a single-abstract-method interface
Know Function, Predicate, Consumer, Supplier and their compositions
Local variables used inside a lambda must be effectively final
pitfalls: Trying to increment a local counter inside a lambda — it won't compile because the variable must be effectively final.

quiz.q: Which functional interface matches `s -> s.isEmpty()` for a String s?
quiz.explain: It takes a String and returns a boolean, which is exactly Predicate<String>.test.

concepts.name: Streams
concepts.summary: Transform collections by describing the steps (filter, map, sorted, collect, groupingBy) instead of writing loops.
concepts.why: Streams express data transformations clearly and appear throughout modern Java codebases.
concepts.body:
A **stream** is a sequence of elements flowing through a **pipeline** of steps: a source, zero or more **intermediate operations** that transform the elements, and one **terminal operation** that produces the result:

```java
List<String> result = orders.stream()        // source
    .filter(o -> o.total() > 100)               // intermediate
    .map(Order::customer)                       // intermediate
    .distinct()
    .sorted()
    .toList();                                  // terminal
```

Intermediate operations are **lazy**: nothing runs until the terminal operation pulls elements through, one at a time. That's why `filter(...).findFirst()` stops as soon as it finds a match.

Common operations:

- Intermediate: `filter`, `map`, `flatMap` (turns each element into several), `distinct`, `sorted`, `limit`, `skip`, `peek` (to look at elements while hunting a bug).
- Terminal: `toList()` (Java 16+, unmodifiable), `forEach`, `count`, `anyMatch`/`allMatch`, `findFirst`, `reduce`, `min`/`max`, and `collect`.

`Collectors` handles the richer needs: `groupingBy(Order::customer)` builds a `Map<K, List<V>>`, optionally with a downstream collector like `counting()` or `summingDouble(...)`; `toMap`, `joining(", ")`, and `partitioningBy`.

For primitives use `IntStream`, `mapToInt(...)`, `sum()`, `average()` — they avoid autoboxing. `IntStream.range(0, n)` replaces many index loops.

Rules to keep in mind:

- A stream can be consumed only once.
- Keep lambdas free of **side effects** (changes to anything outside the lambda); don't add to an external list from `forEach` — collect instead.
- `parallel()` is rarely a win for typical business code; measure before using it.

Streams are not always better than loops. If the pipeline needs complex state, early returns or exceptions the compiler forces you to handle, a plain loop is often clearer.
takeaways: source → lazy intermediate ops → one terminal op
`groupingBy`, `toMap`, `joining` and `partitioningBy` cover most grouping and totalling needs
Use primitive streams for numbers; avoid side effects in lambdas
pitfalls: Reusing a stream after a terminal operation — it throws IllegalStateException.
Building results by adding to an outside list in `forEach` instead of collecting.

quiz.q: When does `list.stream().filter(x -> expensive(x))` call expensive()?
options: Only once a terminal operation runs
quiz.explain: Intermediate operations are lazy; work happens only when a terminal operation pulls elements.

quiz.q: Which collector turns a stream of orders into a Map from customer to list of orders?
quiz.explain: groupingBy classifies elements by a key function and collects each group into a list by default.

concepts.name: Optional
concepts.summary: Return Optional for values that may be absent and handle them with map, orElse, orElseThrow and ifPresent.
concepts.why: Optional makes "might be missing" visible in a method's declared return type and cuts down on NullPointerExceptions.
concepts.body:
**Optional** (`Optional<T>`) is a small holder that either contains one value or is empty. Its main job is as a **return type** for methods that may legitimately find nothing, such as `findUserByEmail`. The return type tells callers they must deal with absence, which a return value that might be `null` never does.

Create one with `Optional.of(value)` (value must be non-null), `Optional.ofNullable(maybeNull)`, or `Optional.empty()`. Streams (see the Streams lesson) return them from `findFirst`, `max`, `min` and `reduce`.

Use it without taking the value out by hand:

- `map(f)` / `flatMap(f)` — transform the value if present.
- `filter(pred)` — keep the value only if it matches.
- `orElse(default)` — fallback value (always evaluated).
- `orElseGet(() -> compute())` — fallback computed only when the Optional is empty.
- `orElseThrow()` — get the value or throw `NoSuchElementException`; `orElseThrow(() -> new NotFound(id))` for your own exception.
- `ifPresent(consumer)` and `ifPresentOrElse(consumer, runnable)`.

Calling `get()` after checking `isPresent()` works but is just null-checking with extra steps; the methods above are more expressive.

Guidelines the JDK designers recommend:

- Use Optional for return values, not for fields, method parameters or collection elements.
- Never return `null` from a method declared to return `Optional`.
- Return an empty collection rather than `Optional<List<T>>`.
- For primitives there are `OptionalInt`, `OptionalLong` and `OptionalDouble`.

Prefer `orElseGet` over `orElse` when the fallback is expensive, such as looking something up in a database — `orElse`'s argument is evaluated even when the value is present.
takeaways: Use Optional as a return type for "may be absent" results
Chain `map`/`filter` and finish with `orElse`, `orElseGet` or `orElseThrow`
Don't use Optional for fields or parameters, and never return null instead of one
pitfalls: Writing `if (opt.isPresent()) return opt.get();` everywhere — it's a null check in disguise.

quiz.q: Why prefer `orElseGet(() -> loadDefault())` over `orElse(loadDefault())`?
options: loadDefault() runs only when the Optional is empty
orElseGet is the only one that handles null
quiz.explain: orElse's argument is evaluated eagerly; orElseGet invokes the supplier only if needed.

concepts.name: Packages, Maven and Gradle
concepts.summary: Organise code into packages, understand the classpath and JARs, and build projects with Maven or Gradle.
concepts.why: Every real Java project uses packages, plus a build tool that compiles the code, fetches the libraries it uses, runs the tests and packages the result.
concepts.body:
In Java, a **package** is a named group of related classes, like a folder. It also keeps names apart, so two libraries can each have a class called `User`. Declare it at the top of the file (`package com.example.billing;`) and put the file in the matching folder, `com/example/billing/`. By convention, package names are your organisation's web address reversed, in lowercase. Use `import` to refer to classes from other packages by their short name; `java.lang` (home of `String` and `Math`) is imported automatically.

While the program runs, the JVM finds classes on the **classpath**: a list of folders and **JAR** files. A JAR is a single zip file of `.class` files plus a short description of its contents. Managing that list by hand quickly becomes painful, which is why everyone uses a **build tool**.

**Maven** and **Gradle** both:

- download the libraries your code uses, its **dependencies** (and the libraries those need in turn), from the public Maven Central store, each named by `groupId:artifactId:version`,
- use the standard layout: `src/main/java`, `src/main/resources`, `src/test/java`,
- compile, run tests and package a JAR with one command.

**Maven** is configured in `pom.xml`, a file that describes the project rather than listing steps, and runs a fixed sequence of phases: `mvn package` compiles, tests and builds the JAR into `target/`. **Gradle** uses a build script, a small program written in Kotlin or Groovy (`build.gradle.kts`), and named tasks: `./gradlew build` puts output in `build/`. Both normally include a small **wrapper** script in the project (`mvnw`, `gradlew`) that downloads the right tool version, so everyone uses the same one.

In Maven, a dependency's *scope* says where it may be used: `test` dependencies such as JUnit (the testing library, next lesson) are available only to test code. In Gradle the equivalent is `testImplementation` versus `implementation`.

Set the Java version explicitly — `<maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>` in Maven, or the `java { toolchain { ... } }` setting in Gradle — so builds don't depend on whichever JDK happens to be installed.
takeaways: Package names mirror directories: `com.example.app` → `com/example/app/`
Build tools fetch dependencies by `groupId:artifactId:version` and use a standard folder layout
Keep the wrapper in the project and set the Java release explicitly, so builds behave the same everywhere
pitfalls: Putting a file in a directory that doesn't match its package declaration, which leads to "class not found" errors.

quiz.q: In Maven, what does `<scope>test</scope>` on a dependency mean?
options: It is available to test code but not packaged with main code
It is downloaded only when tests fail
It replaces the main dependency during tests
It is ignored by the compiler
quiz.explain: Test-scoped dependencies are on the test classpath only, so production code can't use them.

concepts.name: Unit testing with JUnit 5
concepts.summary: Write and run JUnit 5 tests with assertions, assertThrows, setup methods and parameterized tests.
concepts.why: Automated tests let you change code with confidence, and JUnit is the standard testing framework in Java.
concepts.body:
**JUnit 5** (Jupiter) is the standard framework for **unit tests**: small pieces of code that run one part of your program and check the result. Tests live under `src/test/java`, in the same package as the code they test, and run with `mvn test` or `./gradlew test` (Gradle needs `useJUnitPlatform()` in its test task).

A test is a method marked with the **annotation** `@Test`, a marker starting with `@` that JUnit looks for. It passes if it completes without throwing an exception. **Assertions**, checks such as `assertEquals`, throw when an expectation fails:

- `assertEquals(expected, actual)` — expected value first, so failure messages read correctly.
- `assertTrue`, `assertFalse`, `assertNull`, `assertNotNull`.
- `assertThrows(SomeException.class, () -> code())` returns the exception so you can check its message.
- `assertAll(...)` reports several failures at once instead of stopping at the first.

Test classes and methods don't need to be public in JUnit 5. `@BeforeEach` runs before every test (a fresh setup for each), and `@AfterEach` after. JUnit creates a new instance of the test class per test method, so tests don't share instance fields.

**Parameterized tests** run one test with many inputs: annotate with `@ParameterizedTest` and supply data with `@ValueSource`, `@CsvSource` or `@MethodSource`.

Good unit tests are fast, independent and **deterministic**: same result on every run. Structure each as arrange–act–assert, give it a name that states the behaviour (`rejectsNegativeAmounts`), and test one behaviour per method. Code against interfaces (see the Interfaces lesson) so you can pass in simple fake versions; libraries like Mockito (for fakes) and AssertJ (for more readable assertions) are common additions.

Don't chase 100% coverage (the share of your code that tests run). Focus on logic with branches, unusual inputs at the limits, the **edge cases** (empty, null, boundaries), and bugs you have fixed, so they stay fixed.
