takeaways: Annotate with `@Test`; put expected before actual in `assertEquals`
`assertThrows` checks error paths; `@ParameterizedTest` covers many inputs
Each test gets a fresh instance — keep tests independent and fast
pitfalls: Comparing doubles with `assertEquals(a, b)` without an allowed margin of error (a third argument) and failing on tiny rounding differences.

quiz.q: How does JUnit 5 treat instance fields of a test class between two @Test methods?
options: They are shared, so order matters
They are reset to null only if annotated
A new instance is created for each test method
quiz.explain: By default JUnit creates a fresh test class instance per test method, isolating instance state.

concepts.name: Generics in depth: wildcards and erasure
concepts.summary: Use wildcard types with the PECS rule, see why List<Integer> isn't a List<Number>, and learn what type erasure stops generics doing at runtime.
concepts.why: Writing flexible, reusable methods for other people to call, and decoding confusing compile errors, needs a real model of how generics work.
concepts.body:
Even though an `Integer` is a `Number`, a `List<Integer>` is *not* a `List<Number>`: generic types don't inherit from each other that way. If it were, you could add a `Double` to a list of integers through the `List<Number>` view. **Wildcard types** restore flexibility safely:

- `List<? extends Number>` — a list of Number or of *some* type that extends it. You can read elements as `Number`, but can't add (except `null`), because the exact type is unknown.
- `List<? super Integer>` — a list of Integer or a supertype. You can add `Integer`s, but reading only gives you `Object`.
- `List<?>` — any list; read as `Object`.

The rule of thumb is **PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super**. A parameter you read from is a producer (`extends`); one you write into is a consumer (`super`). That's why `Collections.copy` is declared `copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)`, and why comparator parameters are usually `Comparator<? super T>`.

Generics are implemented by **type erasure**: the compiler checks types, then erases type parameters to their bounds (usually `Object`) and inserts casts. At runtime a `List<String>` and a `List<Integer>` are the same class. Consequences:

- No `new T()`, no `new T[n]`, no `instanceof List<String>` — pass a `Class<T>` or a `Supplier<T>` when you need to create instances.
- You can't overload `m(List<String>)` and `m(List<Integer>)`; after erasure they look identical to the JVM.
- Mixing generics with arrays or raw types can let objects of the wrong type into a generic variable, with no error until much later; the compiler warns about this with "unchecked" warnings. Treat those warnings as bugs unless you can prove safety, then suppress narrowly with `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")`.

Use wildcards in method parameters, not in return types — callers shouldn't have to deal with them.
takeaways: `List<Integer>` is not a `List<Number>`; wildcards add the flexibility safely
PECS — read from `? extends T`, write into `? super T`
Type parameters are erased at runtime: no `new T()`, no `instanceof List<String>`
pitfalls: Returning wildcard types from public methods, forcing every caller to handle them.

quiz.q: Which call compiles for a method `void addAll(List<? super Integer> sink)`?
quiz.explain: List<Number> is a list of a supertype of Integer, which is what ? super Integer allows.

quiz.q: Why can't you write `new T[10]` in a generic class?
options: Generic classes can't use arrays at all
T is erased, so the runtime doesn't know which array type to create
quiz.explain: Arrays need their exact component type at runtime, but erasure removes T.

concepts.name: Sealed types and pattern matching
concepts.summary: Model closed hierarchies with sealed interfaces and records, then take them apart with instanceof and switch patterns.
concepts.why: Java 21's pattern matching makes data-oriented code concise and lets the compiler prove you handled every case.
takeaways: `sealed ... permits` closes a hierarchy so the compiler knows every permitted type
Record patterns pull out components; `when` guards refine a case
Switches over sealed types are exhaustive — new permitted types cause compile errors, not runtime bugs
pitfalls: Putting a general case (e.g. `case Rect r`) before a guarded, more specific one — the compiler rejects the dominated case.

quiz.q: A `switch` over a sealed interface covers every permitted record. What happens when a new permitted record is added?
options: It falls into an implicit default
The switch fails to compile until the new type is handled
quiz.explain: Exhaustiveness is checked against the permits list, so the missing case is a compile error.

concepts.name: Threads and thread safety
concepts.summary: Start threads, recognise race conditions, and fix them with synchronized, locks, atomics and concurrent collections.
concepts.why: Web servers, apps with a user interface and big data-processing jobs all do several things at once, and race conditions are among the hardest bugs to find.
concepts.body:
A **thread** is one independent sequence of steps running inside your program. A program can run many at once, which is called **concurrency**. All threads share the same objects in memory, an area called the **heap**. You can start one with `Thread.ofPlatform().start(runnable)` or `new Thread(runnable).start()`, and wait for it with `join()`. In practice you'll usually submit tasks to an executor (next lesson), but the safety rules are the same.

When threads share data that can change (**shared state**), you get **race conditions**: results that depend on the exact timing of the threads. `count++` looks like one indivisible (**atomic**) step but is three steps — read, add, write — and two threads can interleave them so an increment is lost. Worse, without synchronization one thread may never *see* another's writes (more on that in the memory-model lesson).

Tools, from simplest to most specialised:

- **Don't share** mutable state: confine data to one thread, or use immutable objects (records, `List.copyOf`).
- `synchronized` — a method or block that only one thread at a time can run. The thread must first take a **lock** (any object can serve as one) that other threads then wait for; it also makes writes visible to the next thread that takes the same lock.
- **java.util.concurrent.atomic** — `AtomicInteger`, `AtomicLong`, `LongAdder` for counters and updates without locks.
- **Concurrent collections** — `ConcurrentHashMap` (with atomic `merge`, `compute`), `CopyOnWriteArrayList`, `BlockingQueue` for producer-consumer.
- **ReentrantLock** and `ReadWriteLock` when you need to give up after waiting a while (a **timeout**), try once without waiting, or fairness.

Guard **compound actions** too: `if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)` is racy even on a ConcurrentHashMap — use `putIfAbsent` or `computeIfAbsent`.

Keep critical sections short, never call unknown code while holding a lock, and always acquire multiple locks in the same order to avoid **deadlock**, where two threads each wait forever for a lock the other holds.
takeaways: Shared mutable state + no synchronization = race condition
Prefer immutability and confinement; then atomics and concurrent collections; then locks
Make compound actions atomic (`merge`, `computeIfAbsent`), not check-then-act
pitfalls: Assuming `count++` or `HashMap` is safe to use from several threads.
Acquiring two locks in different orders in different places, causing deadlock.

quiz.q: Why can `counter++` on a shared int lose updates?
options: It is a read-modify-write sequence that threads can interleave
quiz.explain: Two threads can both read the same old value and write back the same incremented value.

concepts.name: Executors and thread pools
concepts.summary: Submit tasks to an ExecutorService, collect results with Future, and shut pools down correctly.
concepts.why: Executors separate what to run from how to run it, and are the standard way to do concurrent work in Java.
concepts.body:
Creating raw threads for every task is expensive and unmanageable. An **ExecutorService** accepts tasks and runs them on threads it manages:

- `submit(Runnable)` or `submit(Callable<T>)` returns a **Future<T>**, a placeholder for a result that isn't ready yet; `future.get()` blocks until the result is ready and rethrows a task failure wrapped in `ExecutionException`.
- `invokeAll(tasks)` runs a list of `Callable` tasks and waits for all of them.
- `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n)` suits **CPU-bound** work (pure computation that keeps the processor busy), with `n` near `Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()`.
- `Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(n)` runs tasks after a delay or periodically.
- `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` (Java 21) is the modern choice for **I/O-bound** tasks (ones that mostly wait for files, networks or databases) — see the virtual threads lesson.

An executor must be **shut down**, or its threads keep the program from exiting. Since Java 19 `ExecutorService` is `AutoCloseable`: in a try-with-resources block (a `try (...)` that closes things automatically), `close()` stops accepting tasks and waits for submitted ones to finish. In older code you'll see `shutdown()` followed by `awaitTermination(...)`.

`Future.get()` has an overload with a timeout — use it whenever a stuck task shouldn't hang the caller. `cancel(true)` interrupts a running task; tasks cooperate by checking `Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()` or by letting methods that wait (**blocking** calls) throw `InterruptedException`.

Handle `InterruptedException` properly: either propagate it or restore the flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()`. Swallowing it breaks cancellation.

Beware unlimited queues: a fixed pool fed faster than it can work keeps storing waiting tasks until memory runs out. For servers handling real users (**production**), use `ThreadPoolExecutor` with a bounded queue and a rejection policy, or limit concurrency with a `Semaphore`.
takeaways: Submit tasks to an `ExecutorService` instead of creating threads by hand
Always shut executors down — try-with-resources does it in Java 19+
Use timeouts on `Future.get` and never swallow `InterruptedException`
pitfalls: Forgetting to shut down an executor, so the application never exits.

quiz.q: A task submitted with `submit(callable)` throws an exception. What does `future.get()` do?
options: Nothing; the exception is logged and lost
Throws ExecutionException wrapping the original exception
quiz.explain: Future.get rethrows task failures wrapped in ExecutionException; getCause() gives the original.

concepts.name: CompletableFuture
concepts.summary: Compose asynchronous steps with thenApply, thenCompose, thenCombine, allOf and exceptionally instead of blocking on futures.
concepts.why: Calling several services concurrently and combining their results is a core server-side task, and CompletableFuture is Java's standard tool for it.
concepts.body:
A plain `Future` only lets you wait with `get()`. Real programs often want to be **asynchronous** instead: start slow work, carry on, and handle the result when it arrives. **CompletableFuture** lets you describe what should happen *when* a result arrives, building a pipeline of dependent steps.

Start work with `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(supplier, executor)` (or `runAsync` for no result). Without an executor argument it uses the shared `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`, which is sized for computation — pass your own executor for blocking I/O.

Then chain:

- `thenApply(fn)` — transform the result (like `map`).
- `thenCompose(fn)` — the function itself returns a CompletableFuture; flatten it (like `flatMap`). Use it to chain dependent async calls.
- `thenCombine(other, (a, b) -> ...)` — combine two independent futures.
- `thenAccept(consumer)` — consume the result at the end.
- `allOf(f1, f2, ...)` — completes when all complete; then read each with `join()`. `anyOf` completes on the first.

Errors travel down the chain, skipping the normal steps, until handled with `exceptionally(ex -> fallback)` or `handle((value, ex) -> ...)`. The exception you receive is usually a `CompletionException` wrapping the real cause. `orTimeout(...)` and `completeOnTimeout(value, ...)` add deadlines.

At the edge of your program, `join()` waits and throws unchecked `CompletionException`; `get()` throws exceptions the compiler makes you handle.

Each step runs on whichever thread completed the previous step, or the caller's thread if it was already complete. The `...Async` versions (`thenApplyAsync`) hop to an executor explicitly.

With virtual threads (Java 21), plain blocking code in many threads is often simpler than long async chains. CompletableFuture remains valuable for composing results and for APIs that already return futures, such as `HttpClient.sendAsync`.
takeaways: `thenApply` maps, `thenCompose` chains async calls, `thenCombine` joins two
Handle failures with `exceptionally` or `handle`; they arrive wrapped in CompletionException
Pass your own executor for blocking I/O instead of using the common pool
pitfalls: Calling `join()` right after each `supplyAsync`, which makes the calls sequential again.

quiz.q: You have `CompletableFuture<User> u` and a method `CompletableFuture<List<Order>> ordersOf(User)`. Which gives a `CompletableFuture<List<Order>>`?
quiz.explain: thenApply would produce a nested future; thenCompose flattens a function that returns a CompletableFuture.

concepts.name: Virtual threads
concepts.summary: Run huge numbers of waiting tasks cheaply with Java 21 virtual threads, and avoid their pitfalls: getting stuck on a carrier, pooling, per-thread copies.
concepts.why: Virtual threads let plain, readable code that simply waits handle as much work as complicated asynchronous code, the biggest change to Java concurrency in years.
concepts.body:
A traditional **platform thread** is a thin wrapper over a thread of the **operating system**, the base software that runs the computer. Each one reserves about a megabyte of memory and is managed by the operating system, so a program tops out at a few thousand. A task that spends most of its time waiting, for a database or another service, holds one of those scarce threads the whole time.

A **virtual thread** (final in Java 21) is managed by the JVM. It runs on a small pool of **carrier** platform threads, and when it blocks waiting for input or output (**I/O**), a lock or `sleep`, the JVM unmounts it and frees the carrier for another virtual thread. You can have millions of them.

Creating them:

- `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` — one new virtual thread per task.
- `Thread.ofVirtual().start(runnable)` or `Thread.startVirtualThread(runnable)`.

The programming model is ordinary blocking code: write `var body = client.send(request, ...)`, not **callbacks** (functions you hand over to be called later). Stack traces, debuggers and profilers work as usual.

Guidelines:

- **Don't pool** virtual threads. They are cheap; create one per task. To limit how many tasks use a fragile service at once, use a `Semaphore` (a counter of permits), not a small pool.
- They help **I/O-bound** workloads with many concurrent tasks. CPU-bound work gains nothing — there are still only as many cores.
- In Java 21, blocking inside a `synchronized` block **ties** the virtual thread to its carrier, so frequent long blocking under `synchronized` can starve the carriers. Prefer `ReentrantLock` around blocking calls on Java 21; JDK 24 removed this limitation almost entirely.
- Be careful with `ThreadLocal` (a separate copy of a variable for each thread) used to keep expensive objects around: with a million threads you get a million copies.

Frameworks such as Spring Boot, Helidon and Quarkus can run request handling on virtual threads with a configuration switch.
takeaways: Virtual threads are cheap JVM-managed threads that unmount while blocked
Create one per task; limit access to resources with a Semaphore, not a pool
On Java 21, avoid long blocking inside `synchronized` (it ties the thread to its carrier); use `ReentrantLock`
pitfalls: Using virtual threads for CPU-heavy computation and expecting a speed-up.

quiz.q: What happens when a virtual thread blocks on a socket read (outside synchronized)?
options: The JVM unmounts it so the carrier can run other virtual threads
Its carrier OS thread blocks too
It is converted to a platform thread
quiz.explain: Blocking I/O parks the virtual thread and frees the carrier for other work.

quiz.q: You need at most 20 concurrent calls to a rate-limited API from virtual threads. Best tool?
options: A fixed pool of 20 virtual threads
quiz.explain: Virtual threads shouldn't be pooled; a Semaphore limits concurrency directly.

concepts.name: Annotations and reflection
concepts.summary: Declare and read custom annotations, inspect and invoke code at runtime with reflection, and know the costs.
concepts.why: Frameworks like Spring, JUnit, Jackson and Hibernate are built on annotations and reflection; understanding them demystifies the magic.
concepts.body:
An annotation attaches extra information, **metadata**, to code. Some are for the compiler (`@Override`, `@Deprecated`, `@SuppressWarnings`, `@FunctionalInterface`); most in real projects are read by frameworks (`@Test`, `@Entity`, `@GetMapping`).

Declaring one uses `@interface`, with two meta-annotations that matter:

- `@Retention` — `SOURCE` (discarded by the compiler), `CLASS` (in the class file, the default) or `RUNTIME` (readable via reflection — what frameworks need).
- `@Target` — where it may appear: `TYPE`, `METHOD`, `FIELD`, `PARAMETER`, and more.

Annotation elements look like methods and can have defaults: `String value() default "";`. An element named `value` can be set without a name: `@Route("/home")`.

**Reflection** (`java.lang.reflect`) lets code inspect classes at runtime. Starting from a `Class<?>` object (`obj.getClass()`, `Foo.class`, `Class.forName(name)`), you can list `getDeclaredMethods()`, `getDeclaredFields()` and constructors, read annotations with `getAnnotation(...)`, and call `method.invoke(target, args)` or `constructor.newInstance(...)`. Exceptions thrown by the invoked method arrive wrapped in `InvocationTargetException`.

Costs and limits:

- It bypasses compile-time checks: typos in names fail at runtime.
- It is slower than calling a method directly (though the JVM's optimisations and `MethodHandle`s narrow the gap).
- `setAccessible(true)` on private members is refused for code in another module unless the package is **opened**: Java's module system (see the JPMS lesson) keeps the JDK's internal classes locked away.

Use reflection to build frameworks and tooling, not in everyday business logic. The alternative is annotation-processing tools, which plug into the compiler and generate code before the program runs (Lombok, MapStruct, Dagger).
takeaways: Frameworks need `@Retention(RUNTIME)` annotations to see them via reflection
Reflection inspects and invokes members at runtime, trading safety and speed for flexibility
The module system blocks deep reflection into packages that aren't opened
pitfalls: Forgetting `@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)`, so `getAnnotation` always returns null.

quiz.q: A custom annotation has no @Retention. Can a framework read it with getAnnotation at runtime?
options: No, the default CLASS retention isn't visible to reflection
quiz.explain: The default retention is CLASS: stored in the class file but not exposed through reflection.

concepts.name: Files and I/O with NIO.2
concepts.summary: Read and write files with Path and Files, stream large files line by line, walk folders, and handle charsets correctly.
concepts.why: Almost every application reads settings, writes reports or works through data files.
concepts.body:
Modern file handling uses **NIO.2** (`java.nio.file`). A **Path** represents a location: `Path.of("data", "input.csv")` builds it portably, and `resolve`, `getParent`, `getFileName` and `normalize` manipulate it without touching the disk.

The **Files** utility class does the actual reading and writing, the input/output or **I/O**:

- Small files: `Files.readString(path)`, `Files.readAllLines(path)`, `Files.writeString(path, text)` and `Files.write(path, lines)`.
- Large files: `Files.lines(path)` returns a lazy `Stream<String>`; `Files.newBufferedReader` and `newBufferedWriter` give classic readers and writers.
- Management: `exists`, `createDirectories`, `copy`, `move` (with options like `REPLACE_EXISTING`, `ATOMIC_MOVE`), `delete`, `deleteIfExists`, `size`.
- Directories: `Files.list(dir)` for one level, `Files.walk(dir)` through every subfolder, `Files.find` with a filter.

Streams returned by `lines`, `list` and `walk` keep a file open. The operating system gives each program a limited number of open-file slots, called **file handles**, so always use these streams in try-with-resources. Forgetting this leaks them and eventually fails with "Too many open files".

Text needs a **charset**: the rule for turning characters into bytes and back. Since Java 18 the default is **UTF-8**, which covers every language, everywhere (JEP 400), and the `Files` methods use UTF-8 unless told otherwise. Pass a charset explicitly when reading files from other systems, for example `StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1`.

Write options control behaviour: `StandardOpenOption.APPEND`, `CREATE`, `TRUNCATE_EXISTING`. To avoid readers seeing half-written files, write to a new scratch file in the same directory and `move` it into place with `ATOMIC_MOVE`.

You'll still meet `java.io.File` and `InputStream`/`OutputStream` in older code; `file.toPath()` and `path.toFile()` bridge the two worlds.
takeaways: Use `Path.of` and the `Files` utility methods for file I/O
Close `Files.lines`, `list` and `walk` streams with try-with-resources
UTF-8 is the default since Java 18; specify charsets for foreign files
pitfalls: Using `Files.readAllLines` on multi-gigabyte files and running out of memory — stream them instead.

quiz.q: Why should `Files.lines(path)` be used in try-with-resources?
options: It is required by the compiler
Otherwise lines are returned in random order
The stream holds an open file handle that must be closed
quiz.explain: The lazy stream keeps the file open until closed; leaking it exhausts file descriptors.

concepts.name: The module system (JPMS)
concepts.summary: Describe modules with module-info.java: requires, exports, opens and transitive, and build small runtimes with jlink.
concepts.why: Modules give strong encapsulation for libraries and the JDK itself, and explain the access errors you meet on modern Java.
takeaways: `module-info.java` declares `requires`, `exports` and `opens`
Unexported packages are inaccessible, even for public classes
Classpath code runs in the unnamed module; JDK internals are closed to reflection by default
pitfalls: Silencing reflective-access errors with blanket `--add-opens` flags instead of upgrading the offending library.

quiz.q: A framework must use reflection on private fields in your package but other modules shouldn't compile against it. What do you declare?
quiz.explain: opens grants runtime deep reflection without exporting the package's types for compilation.

concepts.name: Java Memory Model and happens-before
concepts.summary: Understand visibility, reordering and the happens-before rules that make volatile, synchronized and final fields work.
concepts.why: Concurrent code that "works on my machine" can fail on another machine or after the JVM optimises it; the memory model tells you what is actually guaranteed.
concepts.body:
For speed, the compiler, the JVM's **JIT compiler** (which turns busy code into machine code while the program runs) and the processor itself all **reorder** reads and writes of memory, and keep copies of values close at hand in **caches**. Within one thread you can't tell; across threads you can. The **Java Memory Model** (JLS chapter 17) defines which writes another thread is guaranteed to see.

The central idea is **happens-before**. If action A happens-before action B, then B sees A's effects (and everything before A). Key rules:

- Program order: each action in a thread happens-before later actions in that thread.
- Monitor lock: unlocking a monitor happens-before every later lock of the *same* monitor.
- `volatile`: a write to a volatile field happens-before every subsequent read of that field.
- `Thread.start()` happens-before the started thread's actions; a thread's actions happen-before another thread returns from `join()` on it.
- Transitivity ties them together. `java.util.concurrent` classes document their own edges (e.g. putting into a `BlockingQueue` happens-before taking it out).

Two accesses to the same variable from different threads, at least one of them a write, that aren't ordered by happens-before form a **data race**, and the reading thread may see stale values indefinitely. A classic failure: a `boolean running` flag checked over and over in a loop (**polling**) without `volatile` — the JIT may hoist the read out of the loop and spin forever.

`volatile` gives visibility and ordering but not atomicity: `volatile int x; x++` is still racy. Use atomics for that.

**final fields** have a special guarantee: if the object reference doesn't escape during construction, every thread sees the final fields' constructed values without synchronization. That is what makes immutable objects safe to share.

Double-checked locking, a technique for creating a shared single instance (a **singleton**) only when first needed, works only if the field is `volatile`. The simpler alternative is the holder-class idiom shown below, which relies on Java's guarantee that a class is initialised exactly once.
takeaways: Without a happens-before edge, another thread may see stale or reordered values
Edges come from locks, volatile, thread start/join and java.util.concurrent classes
`volatile` gives visibility, not atomicity; final fields make safe immutable objects
pitfalls: Polling a non-volatile flag from another thread, which can loop forever after JIT optimisation.
Double-checked locking without `volatile` on the instance field.

quiz.q: Thread A writes `data = 42` and then writes volatile `ready = true`. Thread B reads `ready == true`, then reads `data`. What does B see?
options: 42 — guaranteed by the volatile happens-before edge
Whatever is in its CPU cache
quiz.explain: The volatile write happens-before the read that sees it, and program order carries the earlier data write along.

quiz.q: Which is still a data race?
options: Reading a final field of a properly constructed immutable object
Accessing a field only inside synchronized blocks on the same lock
Incrementing a volatile int from two threads
quiz.explain: volatile ensures visibility, but x++ is a read-modify-write that two threads can interleave.

concepts.name: Garbage collection and the heap
concepts.summary: How the JVM reclaims memory: reachability, young and old objects, G1, ZGC and Parallel collectors, heap sizing and memory leaks.
concepts.why: Sudden slow responses, OutOfMemoryErrors and memory limits in containers all come down to understanding the heap and the collector.
concepts.body:
Objects live on the **heap**, the JVM's shared pool of memory; local variables live on each thread's own stack. An object can be collected once it is no longer **reachable** from a **GC root**, a starting point the collector treats as in use: local variables of running methods, static fields, and references held by native code. Objects that only refer to each other in a cycle don't keep each other alive; reachability is what counts.

Most collectors divide the heap by object age, based on the observation that most objects die young. New objects go to the **young generation**, collected often and cheaply by copying the few survivors; objects that survive several collections are transferred to the old generation, collected less often.

Collectors in **HotSpot**, the standard JVM, as of Java 21:

- **G1** (default) — divides the heap into regions, does most of its work while the program keeps running, aims at a pause-time goal (`-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis`, default 200 ms). A good default for most services.
- **ZGC** (`-XX:+UseZGC`) — almost fully concurrent, pauses typically under a millisecond regardless of heap size. Java 21 added generational ZGC via `-XX:+ZGenerational`, which later became the only mode.
- **Parallel** (`-XX:+UseParallelGC`) — the most work done per second (**throughput**), but with longer pauses that freeze the whole program; good for big offline data-processing jobs.
- **Serial** — single-threaded, for tiny heaps and small containers.

Size the heap with `-Xmx` / `-Xms`, or in containers with `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75`. Leave headroom: thread stacks, class data, compiled code and some I/O memory live outside the heap.

A Java **memory leak** is memory held by objects kept reachable by accident: an ever-growing static map or cache, listeners never removed, ThreadLocals on pooled threads. The symptom is old-generation usage that climbs after each collection until `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`. Use `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` and open the dump in a heap analyser to see which objects keep the most memory alive.

Turn on GC logging (a running record of every collection) in your live system with `-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log` — it's cheap and invaluable.
takeaways: Objects are collected when unreachable from GC roots — cycles don't leak
G1 is the default; ZGC for very low latency, Parallel for throughput
Leaks are accidental references (static maps, listeners, ThreadLocals); diagnose with heap dumps and GC logs
pitfalls: Setting `-Xmx` equal to the container memory limit, leaving no room for non-heap memory and getting OOM-killed.

quiz.q: Two objects reference each other but nothing else references either. What happens?
quiz.explain: Java's tracing collectors use reachability from roots, so unreachable cycles are collected.

quiz.q: A latency-sensitive service with a 32 GB heap suffers 300 ms pauses. Which change is most likely to help?
quiz.explain: ZGC does nearly all work concurrently and keeps pauses sub-millisecond independent of heap size.

concepts.name: Bytecode and javap
concepts.summary: Read the JVM's stack-based bytecode with javap, and see how method calls, lambdas and string concatenation really compile.
concepts.why: Reading bytecode settles debates about what the compiler actually generates and underlies the tools that measure or rewrite running code.
concepts.body:
`javac` compiles to **bytecode**, the instruction set of the JVM. Inspect it with the **javap** tool: `javap -c -p MyClass.class`. Adding `-v` also shows the **constant pool**, the table of names and fixed values the class refers to.

The JVM is a **stack machine**. Each running method gets numbered **local variable slots** (slot 0 is `this` in instance methods) and an **operand stack**, a scratch pile that instructions push values onto and take them off. `a + b` on two `int`s becomes `iload_1`, `iload_2`, `iadd`, `istore_3`. Instruction prefixes encode types: `i` = `int`, `l` = `long`, `d` = `double`, `a` = reference.

Method calls come in five flavours, and knowing them explains a lot of language behaviour:

- `invokestatic` — static methods.
- `invokevirtual` — ordinary instance methods, dispatched on the runtime class (polymorphism).
- `invokeinterface` — calls through an interface type.
- `invokespecial` — constructors (`<init>`) and `super.` calls: no dynamic dispatch. (Since Java 11, calls to private methods use `invokevirtual`, a by-product of how nested classes now share access.)
- **invokedynamic** — the target is chosen while the program runs, by a setup method (the bootstrap method). Lambdas use it (via `LambdaMetafactory`), and so does string concatenation since Java 9 (`StringConcatFactory`).

Other details become visible too: generics are erased to their bounds with `checkcast` inserted at use sites; autoboxing turns into `Integer.valueOf` and `intValue()` calls; a `switch` on strings becomes a `hashCode` lookup followed by `equals`; constructors and **static initializers** (code that runs once when a class is first used) appear as `<init>` and `<clinit>`.

The class file also carries the **constant pool** (names, literals, method references), a version number (65 for Java 21) and extra sections such as line-number tables, which let stack traces show line numbers.

Libraries like ASM and ByteBuddy generate and rewrite bytecode — that's how Mockito makes fake objects for tests, how Hibernate makes stand-in objects that load data on demand, and how Java agents (add-ons loaded into a JVM) change code as it loads. A standard Class-File API arrived as a preview after Java 21.
takeaways: The JVM is a stack machine: locals in slots, work on an operand stack
invokestatic, invokevirtual, invokeinterface, invokespecial and invokedynamic encode call semantics
Lambdas and string concatenation are linked at runtime through invokedynamic
pitfalls: Assuming source-level features like generics exist at runtime — `javap` shows they're erased to casts.

quiz.q: An override calls `super.toString()`. Which instruction does javac emit for that call?
quiz.explain: super calls must bypass dynamic dispatch to reach the parent's implementation, so they use invokespecial.

quiz.q: How is a lambda expression implemented in bytecode?
options: As a separate anonymous .class file generated by javac
As an invokedynamic call site whose bootstrap creates the functional object at runtime
As a static field initialised in <clinit>
quiz.explain: javac emits the body as a private method and an invokedynamic site bootstrapped by LambdaMetafactory.

concepts.name: Class loading and initialization
concepts.summary: Follow a class through loading, linking and initialization; understand class loaders, delegation and NoClassDefFoundError.
concepts.why: Clashing library versions on the classpath, apps that load add-ons, servers that host several apps, and startup time all hinge on how classes are loaded.
concepts.body:
The JVM loads classes **lazily**, the first time they are needed. Each class goes through three phases (JVMS chapter 5):

- **Loading** — a **class loader** finds the class's compiled bytes (in a JAR, a folder, over the network, or generated on the fly) and creates a `Class` object.
- **Linking** — *verification* checks the bytecode is well-formed and uses types correctly; *preparation* sets aside memory for static fields, filled with default values; *resolution* replaces the names of other classes and methods with direct pointers, often only when first used.
- **Initialization** — runs the static initializer `<clinit>`: static field assignments and `static { }` blocks, in source order. It happens on first active use (creating an instance, calling a static method, reading a non-constant static field) and is guaranteed to run exactly once, even if several threads arrive at the same moment.

Class loaders form a hierarchy: the **bootstrap** loader (core `java.base` classes), the **platform** loader (other JDK modules), and the **application** (system) loader (your classpath or module path). Loaders use **parent delegation**: they hand the job to (**delegate** to) their parent first, and only load the class yourself if the parent can't. That stops applications from replacing `java.lang.String`.

A class's runtime identity is its name **plus its defining loader**. The same class loaded by two loaders gives two distinct types — the source of baffling `ClassCastException: Foo cannot be cast to Foo` in app servers and plugin systems.

Know the two errors apart:

- `ClassNotFoundException` — a checked exception from explicit loading (`Class.forName`) when the class can't be found.
- `NoClassDefFoundError` — the class was present when the code was compiled but is missing when it runs, *or* its static initializer previously failed (the first attempt throws `ExceptionInInitializerError`).

Startup time is dominated by loading and verifying classes. **Class Data Sharing** (CDS, on by default for JDK classes; `-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit` for your app) maps pre-parsed classes from an archive to speed it up.
takeaways: Classes are loaded lazily: load, link (verify, prepare, resolve), initialize
Loaders delegate to their parent first; class identity = name + defining loader
NoClassDefFoundError means missing at runtime or a previously failed static initializer
pitfalls: Throwing from a static initializer: the first use gets ExceptionInInitializerError, every later use NoClassDefFoundError.

quiz.q: Reading `Config.NAME`, where `static final String NAME = "app";`, from another class:
options: Throws if Config isn't loaded yet
Loads Config with a new class loader
Does not initialize Config, because the constant is inlined at compile time
quiz.explain: Compile-time constants are copied into the using class's constant pool, so no initialization is triggered.

concepts.name: JIT compilation and warm-up
concepts.summary: How HotSpot interprets, profiles and compiles hot code with C1 and C2: inlining, escape analysis, deoptimization and warm-up.
concepts.why: The JIT compiler explains why Java gets faster after startup, why naive speed tests (benchmarks) lie, and which code shapes run fast.
concepts.body:
**HotSpot**, the standard JVM, starts by **interpreting** bytecode (carrying out one instruction at a time) while collecting a **profile**: how often each method and loop runs, which branches are taken, which concrete classes of object (the **receiver**, the object a method is called on) appear at each call. Busy ("hot") code is then compiled to **machine code**, the processor's own instructions, by the **JIT** (just-in-time) compiler. With **tiered compilation** (the default):

- **C1** compiles quickly with light optimisation, so code speeds up soon after startup.
- **C2** later recompiles the hottest methods with aggressive, profile-guided optimisation.

Key optimisations:

- **Inlining** — copying a callee's body into the caller. It is the gateway to every other optimisation. Small methods and getters cost nothing once inlined, so write clear small methods.
- **Devirtualization** — if a call site has only ever seen one or two receiver types (monomorphic or bimorphic), C2 inlines them behind a cheap type check. Megamorphic sites (many types) stay as slower calls that look up the method each time.
- **Escape analysis** — if an object is never seen outside one method, C2 can skip creating it on the heap and keep its fields in the processor's fastest storage (registers).
- Loop optimisations: range-check elimination, unrolling and auto-vectorisation.

These optimisations are **speculative**. If an assumption breaks — a new subclass gets loaded, or a never-taken branch is taken — the JVM **deoptimizes**: it discards the compiled code, falls back to interpreting and recompiles later.

Consequences: a JVM application needs a **warm-up** period before reaching peak speed, so measure after warm-up and use **JMH** (the Java Microbenchmark Harness) to time small pieces of code; it also stops the JIT from deleting code whose result is never used. `-XX:+PrintCompilation` shows methods as they are compiled, and JDK Flight Recorder (JFR) logs compilation and deoptimization events. For startup-sensitive workloads, CDS archives, Project Leyden work and GraalVM native image do the work before the program starts.
takeaways: Code runs interpreted first; hot methods are compiled by C1, then C2 using profiles
Inlining enables everything else; small methods are effectively free
Speculative optimisations can be undone (deoptimization) — always benchmark after warm-up
pitfalls: Timing a loop once with `System.nanoTime()` and drawing conclusions — you measure the interpreter and the JIT, not your code.

quiz.q: What usually happens to an instance call site that has only ever seen one receiver class?
options: It is always a virtual table lookup
It is compiled by C1 only
C2 inlines the target behind a cheap type guard
It is converted to invokestatic in the class file
quiz.explain: Monomorphic call sites are devirtualized and inlined, guarded by a type check that deoptimizes if violated.

concepts.name: Performance tuning and profiling
concepts.summary: Find real bottlenecks with JFR, JDK Mission Control, jcmd and JMH, and fix the usual suspects: allocation, locks, I/O and GC.
concepts.why: Guessing at performance problems wastes time; measuring with the JDK's own tools finds the actual cause quickly.
concepts.body:
The first rule of performance work is **measure, don't guess**. Define the target: for example the response time that 99% of requests beat (p99 **latency**, a **percentile**), work done per second (throughput), or memory use. Reproduce the problem under realistic load, then find the **bottleneck**, the one slow part that holds everything up.

The JDK ships excellent tools:

- **JDK Flight Recorder (JFR)** — a low-overhead event recorder built into the JVM, safe to run on your live system. Start it with `-XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=rec.jfr`, or turn it on in an already running JVM with `jcmd <pid> JFR.start` (`<pid>` is the running program's ID number). It logs which code is using the processor, which objects are being created, GC pauses, threads waiting for locks, I/O and what each thread is doing.
- **JDK Mission Control (JMC)** — a desktop app for analysing `.jfr` files; the `jfr` command (`jfr print`, `jfr summary`) works too.
- **jcmd** — the Swiss army knife for a running JVM: `Thread.print` (thread dump), `GC.heap_info`, `GC.heap_dump`, `VM.flags`, `VM.native_memory`.
- Separate **profilers** (tools that measure where time goes) such as async-profiler draw **flame graphs**: pictures showing which methods use the most processor time or create the most objects.

For small pieces of code, use **JMH** (Java Microbenchmark Harness). It handles warm-up, starts fresh JVMs, and prevents the JIT from eliminating or hoisting the code under test — pitfalls that make hand-written timing loops meaningless.

Typical findings and fixes:

- **Allocation pressure** — creating (allocating) too many short-lived objects keeps the GC busy: autoboxing in busy loops, needless copies, building strings with `+` in loops. Use primitives, reuse objects, and create collections at their final size.
- **Lock contention** — threads queuing for the same lock. JFR's lock events point at the busy ones; hold locks for less time, use concurrent collections, or avoid sharing.
- **I/O waits** — combine many small calls into fewer large ones, keep copies of results you reuse, reuse open database connections, or use virtual threads so the waits overlap.
- **GC** — check GC logs for pause times and frequency before reaching for flags; often the fix is allocating less or sizing the heap correctly.

Change one thing at a time, re-measure, and keep the benchmark so regressions are caught later.
takeaways: Measure first: reproduce, profile, change one thing, re-measure
JFR + JMC and jcmd are built in and safe for production diagnostics
Use JMH for microbenchmarks — hand-written timing loops lie
pitfalls: Tuning JVM flags before profiling, when the real problem is allocation or contention in application code.

quiz.q: Why is JMH preferred over timing a loop with System.nanoTime()?
options: JMH handles warm-up, forking and prevents JIT dead-code elimination from skewing results
JMH runs code in the interpreter for fairness
quiz.explain: Without those controls the JIT can optimise away or hoist the measured code and warm-up distorts timings.
